clue.text: You shouldn't have holiday sex with wretched Keir to please yourself

parts.note: what someone says on being given a present, so it stands for TA, informal British for thanks

indicators.note: wretched means in a sorry, broken state, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
leave is time off work, a holiday
it is a coy word for sex, as in 'doing it'

explanation.surface: A tabloid warning: don't go on holiday and sleep with a miserable Keir Starmer just to please yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' is what you say on receiving a gift, so it stands for British slang thanks. 'Wretched' tells you to rearrange the Labour leader's name with 'to', and 'holiday sex' supplies the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom offers a take-it-or-not choice with no compromise, the same shrug as telling someone to suit themselves.

clue.text: Labour introducing shifting scale that makes sparks fly

indicators.note: Labour introducing says the word for labour takes the next letters into itself

parts.note: toil is hard work, labour

indicators.note: shifting letters move about, so the word scale is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Labour Party brings in a sliding scale that sets off fiery arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the political party; it is plain work, TOIL, which takes in ESLAC from 'shifting' scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tesla coil is an electrical transformer producing very high voltages, famous for throwing out dramatic arcs of electricity.

clue.text: Orderly looked after nurses close to sanatorium

indicators.note: to nurse a patient is to hold them in your care, so this word wraps itself round what follows

parts.note: to look after a thing is to keep it

indicators.note: the close of a word is where it finishes, and only that final letter is wanted

parts.note: the letter the word finishes on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a hospital ward, where an orderly is a member of staff. The definition wants the adjective, a word almost nobody uses except with un- in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Orderly -> KEMPT: kempt describes hair or a person combed and tidy, a sense that survives mainly in its negative and in crosswords.

clue.text: Third off price for ham?

parts.note: the third letter of price is I, and a ham, an amateur radio operator, says that letter with its NATO phonetic code word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Third off price' reads like a discount at the deli counter, but the ham is a radio ham, and the third letter of 'price' is what they spell out phonetically.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet used by radio amateurs, the code word for the letter I is the name of a large Asian country.

clue.text: One beastly Conservative's unguarded kiss

indicators.note: unguarded means stripped of the guards on either side, so the outer letters go

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party, here with the possessive S attached
X is the conventional written kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A beastly Tory lets slip a careless kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unguarded' removes the first and last letters of TORYS, leaving ORY, then X follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An oryx is a large straight-horned African antelope, so one beast is a fair description.

clue.text: Key expert's cant in hearing

indicators.note: what is taken in hearing is judged by ear alone, so the spelling you write down need not be the spelling you were given

parts.note: to cant is to tilt, and a ship that tilts is said to list; that is the word being spoken

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a locksmith or a piano tuner talking jargon. 'Cant' also means insincere talk, which is the sense the clue wants you to hear first.
explanation.definitionFit: Key expert -> LISZT: the Hungarian virtuoso was the supreme master of the piano keyboard, so the definition names him by the black and white keys.

clue.text: TV show possibly exposed sporting star as one who gets high

indicators.note: this warns that what follows is only one possible member of the class, not the class itself
something exposed has had its covering taken off, and a word's covering is the letter at each end
to sport a hat or a tan is to wear it, so whatever is sported is worn on the outside of the other piece

parts.note: the A-list is where the famous names sit, so an A-lister is a star
a SERIAL is one kind of TV show, with the letter at each end taken off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting star' reads as an athlete and wants a celebrity, and 'one who gets high' points at a trapeze rather than a habit.
explanation.definitionFit: one who gets high -> AERIALIST: an aerialist performs on the trapeze or the high wire, so getting high is literally the job description.

clue.text: Europeans disturbed by news on international lack of interest

indicators.note: what disturbs you gets inside you, so this piece lands in the middle of the one before it
in a down entry one thing sits on another by being written above it, so what follows goes underneath

parts.note: the union the Europeans built, in its two-letter form
N is the abbreviation for new, and a doubled letter is how crosswords write its plural
I is the standard short form of international, as on a fixture list

explanation.walkthrough: Being disturbed by news is what happens to a reader and what happens to the letters, which is the whole of the surface's trick.
explanation.definitionFit: lack of interest -> ENNUI: the French loan word for a listless boredom in which nothing seems worth attending to, stronger than ordinary idleness.

clue.text: Cover of The Modern Age sampling Queen track

indicators.note: sampling a record drops a piece of one track into the middle of another, and these letters do the same
a cover is what goes round the outside, so the letters wanted are the ones at either edge

parts.note: the letters at the two edges of the word, its covers
AD, anno domini, is the era we are still counting in
R for Regina, the Latin the monarch signs with

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make The Modern Age one Strokes title, and the wordplay refuses to read it that way: the first word and the other two are handled separately.
explanation.definitionFit: track -> TREAD: the pattern moulded into a tyre is its tread, and the marks it leaves are tracks, so the two words meet on the road.

clue.text: One quits newspapers possibly drowning in sauce sooner or later

indicators.note: someone who quits walks out and does not come back, and the letter beside it goes the same way
what drowns goes under the surface of the liquid, so this piece ends up inside the other

parts.note: soy is the sauce in the little bottle on the table

indicators.note: a warning that the word before it names only one possible member of a wider class

parts.note: newspapers are one branch of the media
the Roman numeral for one, and the letter that walks out

explanation.walkthrough: The 'one' quitting is a numeral rather than a resigning journalist, and 'possibly' is the flag that newspapers stand for something broader.
explanation.definitionFit: sooner or later -> SOMEDAY: both phrases promise a future occasion while refusing to name it, which is what makes them interchangeable.

clue.text: To choke, losing heart in Wimbledon, is hard to explain

indicators.note: what you lose you no longer have, so those letters do not reach the answer
the heart of a word is the letter at its exact centre, which only an odd-numbered word has

parts.note: to choke someone is to STRANGLE them, and this is that verb with one letter pulled out
nine letters, so the fifth stands at the dead centre

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a player bottling it on Centre Court, and Wimbledon is in the clue to be counted rather than played.
explanation.definitionFit: hard to explain -> STRANGE: what is strange resists explanation because it matches no pattern you already hold, which is why the two phrases swap.

clue.text: Vauxhall car approaching yard is off course

indicators.note: what approaches comes right up against the thing it nears, so these letters sit immediately in front

parts.note: the Astra is Vauxhall's long-running family hatchback
Y is the abbreviation for a yard on a ruler

explanation.walkthrough: Vauxhall is a car marque, a London district and a football ground; only the badge on the bonnet is wanted here.
explanation.definitionFit: off course -> ASTRAY: a ship off course has wandered from the route it meant to take, and going astray is that same straying, on land or in morals.

clue.text: Made firm second date arranged with bombshell

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the word date is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
an IED, an improvised explosive device, is a homemade bomb

explanation.surface: A second date was set up with a stunning woman, making the relationship firmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombshell' suggests a glamorous date; it is a literal bomb, the improvised explosive device familiar from news reports, placed after the rearranged date.
explanation.definitionFit: To steady something is to stop it wobbling and make it stable, so made firm is its past tense.

clue.text: American woman who won five Grand Slam titles

definitions.text: who won five Grand Slam titles

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American
the pronoun you use of a woman

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is two small pieces, so the whole clue rests on one false statement: it calls the player a woman, and the player was not one.
explanation.definitionFit: who won five Grand Slam titles -> ASHE: Arthur Ashe took three singles majors and two more in doubles, five in all, at the height of the 1970s.

clue.text: Republicans originally redacted models' faces

indicators.note: the first letter is struck out, as a censor blacks out text

parts.note: the GOP (Grand Old Party) is the US Republican Party
models strike poses

explanation.surface: Political censorship: party members blur out the faces of fashion models.
explanation.walkthrough: GOP is the American Republican Party; with its opening letter blacked out it gives OP.
explanation.definitionFit: To face an opponent is to confront or stand against them, as in opposing them.

clue.text: Character from The Odyssey that's acidic?

parts.note: how acid a liquid is gets measured on the pH scale
Roman one: a reading of 1 on that scale is about as acid as liquids get

explanation.walkthrough: Homer wrote in Greek, so a character from his poem is a letter of that alphabet rather than a hero. The scale runs 0 to 14, and the numeral is written the Roman way.
explanation.definitionFit: Character from The Odyssey -> PHI: the poem is Greek, so its characters in the typographic sense are the letters of the Greek alphabet, of which this is one.

clue.text: Four times Sugar wasted capital in Baden-Württemberg

indicators.note: something laid waste is left in ruins, and letters in ruins keep none of their original order

parts.note: t is the scientist's symbol for time, and four of them are asked for
the whole word goes into the mix

explanation.walkthrough: The Sugar of the surface is Alan, and 'four times' looks like a frequency until you notice that time has a one-letter symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: capital in Baden-Württemberg -> STUTTGART: the seat of government of that German state, home to Mercedes and Porsche, named here by its region rather than its country.

clue.text: Extremely cool remix of Strokes' Last Nite for those that pay

indicators.note: the extremes of the word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept
a remix reworks a track, so these letters are rearranged
only the final letter of the band's name is used

explanation.surface: Praises a slick remix of the Strokes song Last Nite, aimed at paying listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: Last Nite is a real Strokes song, but the title splits: 'Last' is an instruction on the band's name, and only 'Nite' joins the mix as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Clients are customers who pay for a professional's services.

clue.text: Meloni's opener: "Trump's intelligence? Zero!"

parts.note: the Central Intelligence Agency answers to the American president
a nought is written as a round O

explanation.walkthrough: Giorgia Meloni is Italy's prime minister, so the word she opens with is Italian, and the surface's joke about presidential intelligence is doing the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Meloni's opener -> CIAO: the Italian greeting an Italian speaker leads with, and the same word again on parting.

clue.text: Collar's missing a zip

indicators.note: missing a says the letter a is absent from the word for collar

parts.note: to collar a suspect is to catch them, as is to nail them; the 's is 'is', so collar is missing a

explanation.surface: A shirt collar has lost its zip fastener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collar' and 'zip' both look like clothing; collar is the verb to catch, and zip is slang for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip is informal for nothing at all, the same as a score of zero in sport.

clue.text: Insignificant banker's unacceptable service on the back of jet

indicators.note: riding on the back of a thing means coming along behind it, so these letters follow rather than lead

parts.note: a jet of water is a stream of it
a serve that clips the net is a let and will not be accepted, so it is taken again

explanation.walkthrough: Banker for river is one of the oldest crossword conventions, on the grounds that a river is the thing with banks; the surface's bonus and bank job are decoys.
explanation.definitionFit: Insignificant banker -> STREAMLET: the banker is a watercourse, and the -let ending shrinks it to something too small to matter.

clue.text: The French certain to embrace current convenient opportunity

indicators.note: an embrace closes arms round whoever is held, so the letters go one on each side of what follows

parts.note: the definite article as the French write it
someone certain of a thing is sure of it
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current

explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' is the electrical kind, not the present-day kind, and the French article is a crossword staple worth banking alongside LA and LES.
explanation.definitionFit: convenient opportunity -> LEISURE: at your leisure means whenever it suits you, so the noun names time free to be used as you choose.

clue.text: Tips from angry sub: "Trying your luck annoys readers wanting columns"

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its topmost point, so one letter comes off the front of each word named

parts.words: angry sub: "Trying your luck annoys readers
parts.note: the seven words each hand over the letter they begin with, in the order they are printed

explanation.walkthrough: A sub-editor's columns are inches of newsprint and an architect's are pillars, which is the whole of the joke; the quoted grumble is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: wanting columns -> ASTYLAR: the architect's word for a front built without pillars, from the Greek stylos, a column, with the negative a- in front.

clue.text: United's lead cut by player's mistake …

indicators.note: something that cuts into a thing lands in the middle of it, splitting what it enters

parts.note: the lead you walk a dog on is a tether
OG is how a scoreline records an own goal

explanation.walkthrough: The capital U makes it a football club and the ellipsis runs the sentence on into 25 across, so nothing in the surface admits it is a clue about dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: United -> TOGETHER: to stand united is to stand as one, which is what doing anything together means; the club name is the misdirection.

clue.text: Half-hearted old Tory enforcer upset region in dispute

indicators.note: a word with twin letters at its heart can be halved there, and only one of the pair survives
something upset has been tipped over, so the letters are read in the opposite order

parts.note: Norman TEBBIT was the Conservatives' chairman and hard man, here with one of the twins at his centre gone

explanation.walkthrough: Tebbit was Margaret Thatcher's party chairman, the 'on yer bike' man; the setter likes the name for the pair of letters sitting at its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: region in dispute -> TIBET: the Himalayan territory China governs and a government-in-exile claims, so the definition names it by that unresolved status.

clue.text: Eagle going around after golf class

indicators.note: a thing going around comes back the way it went, so its letters run in the opposite order
what comes after follows on behind, which in a down entry means further down the column

parts.note: an ERNE is a sea eagle, its four letters turned about
golf is how the radio alphabet says G

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a round of golf, where an eagle is two under par; the wordplay wants the bird, and the erne is the crossword's standard one.
explanation.definitionFit: class -> GENRE: a genre is a class of books, films or music grouped by shared form, so one noun of category stands for the other.

clue.text: Space kept by priest for fragrant resin

indicators.note: whatever is kept by someone is held within their keeping, so this piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Eli is the Old Testament priest who brought up Samuel
an em is the printer's space, as wide as the letter M is cast

explanation.walkthrough: Two conventions worth banking: the biblical three-letter priest, and the typesetter's em, which turns up whenever a clue mentions space or width.
explanation.definitionFit: fragrant resin -> ELEMI: elemi is the soft aromatic gum tapped from canarium trees in the Philippines and used in varnishes and incense.

clue.text: … short cross Rayan Aït-Nouri initially returned back to Donnarumma for City

indicators.note: short means the word for cross loses its last letter

parts.note: an ankh is the Egyptian looped cross

indicators.note: returned means the picked letters are read in the opposite direction
initially asks for the player's initials, the first letter of the forename and of the hyphenated surname

parts.note: first letters of Rayan and of the surname Aït-Nouri, which counts as one name, so its second half gives nothing

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of Donnarumma

explanation.surface: Continuing 22: Aït-Nouri's short cross is played back to goalkeeper Donnarumma, both of Manchester City.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 22 Across, a football commentary. 'Short' trims ANKH to ANK; the player's initials are RA, since Aït-Nouri is one surname, and 'returned' turns them to AR; 'back to' Donnarumma gives A.
explanation.definitionFit: Ankara is the capital of Turkey, an example of a city, while the surface's City is the football club.

clue.text: New York city cops heading to apprehend animal

indicators.note: to cop something is to catch and keep it, so this piece is taken inside
the heading of a word is the letter at its top, and only that one is taken

parts.note: the state's two-letter postal abbreviation
LA is the shorthand for Los Angeles
the letter this word starts with

explanation.walkthrough: 'New York city cops' reads as one police force and splits into two separate abbreviations, while 'cops' turns from a noun into the verb that does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: animal -> NYALA: definition by example, since the nyala is one particular spiral-horned antelope of southern Africa rather than the class of animals.

clue.text: Gay, maybe rampant and single!

indicators.note: a flag that the word before it is only one possible bearer of the name, not the name's meaning
a heraldic beast rampant is reared up on its hind legs, so the letters stand up the other way

parts.note: the B-29 that carried the Hiroshima bomb was the Enola Gay, named for the pilot's mother

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is there to keep you reading 'gay' as an adjective; the wordplay wants the surname, and the first name that famously goes in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: single -> ALONE: single here means unaccompanied rather than unmarried, the sense of a person with nobody else present.

clue.text: Huxley's soporific book on revolution

indicators.note: a revolution turns a thing full circle, so what was written one way comes out the other

parts.note: AMOS is one of the twelve minor prophets and a book of the Old Testament in its own right

explanation.walkthrough: Short books of the Bible are worth learning as spare letters, and 'revolution' keeps the surface political while doing something purely mechanical.
explanation.definitionFit: Huxley's soporific -> SOMA: in Brave New World soma is the state-issued pill that dulls every citizen into contentment, a drug Huxley invented and named.

clue.text: Who's licensed to kill twisted, barely legal kink?

parts.note: James Bond, agent 007, holds a licence to kill

indicators.note: twisted means turned round, so the middle letters are read in reverse
barely means stripped bare of the outer letters, leaving the middle of legal

parts.note: middle letters of legal

explanation.surface: A question about James Bond's twisted taste for barely legal kinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely legal' looks like a phrase about age of consent; read literally, 'barely' strips the word to its middle, and 'twisted' turns that round after the spy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bondage, being tied up for sexual pleasure, is a common fetish, which is what kink means here.

clue.text: List of elite US students said to be doing well

indicators.note: what is said is heard rather than read, so the letters you write need only match the sound

parts.note: American schools post an honor roll of their best students, and an English mouth drops the aitch and runs the words together

explanation.walkthrough: The American spelling matters: an honour roll would not sound the same. Said aloud without the aitch, the words re-divide into a different phrase entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: doing well -> ON A ROLL: the idiom for a run of success, borrowed from a gambler whose dice keep coming good.

clue.text: Professional representative could be awful charlatan getting cut repeatedly: first 12.5% of earnings

indicators.note: awful suggests something mangled, so all these letters are rearranged
the word is cut short more than once, losing its last two letters
one eighth of an eight-letter word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Warns that a talent agent may be a dreadful fraud who keeps taking an eighth of the client's earnings.
explanation.walkthrough: GETTING trimmed twice gives GETTI; 'earnings' has eight letters, so 12.5% of it is E. These join CHARLATAN in the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical agent represents actors professionally, finding them work for a commission.
